# The Mission System: Land, Labour, and Records {#sec-2-01}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act II — Land, Monopoly, and Institution · 1769–1821
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does power begin before markets exist?

**The answer.** It begins with a ledger. Spain took Alta California without a
settler population, an economy, or a market, and held it by writing everything
down — baptisms, marriages, burials, rations, labour. California's first form of
power was legibility: the conversion of human lives into administrative entries,
by an institution that owned the only pen.

**The mechanism.** Chokepoint control of the record. The mission is the book's
first data centre, and the argument it opens is the one Act V closes: whoever
holds the register decides who exists in an official sense. Also public
authority and private benefit fused from the start — the Crown's mandate, the
order's land, the Indigenous labour.

**The key fact.** Mission San Francisco de Asís was founded in 1776, at what is
now 320 Dolores Street. The building is still there. It is the oldest intact
structure in San Francisco, and it was an accounting office as much as a church.

**The human anchor.** A page from a mission baptismal register: a name assigned,
a date, a parentage recorded, an original name absent. One line is the entire
mechanism.

**Excluded voices.** The Ohlone, Chumash, and dozens of other peoples, who
appear in the foundational documents of California almost exclusively as entries
— enumerated, renamed, and set to work. The population collapse in the mission
districts is the central fact of this chapter and must not be a footnote to it.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that administrative capacity precedes economic
power by showing that Spain controlled Alta California for fifty years with
almost no settlers, using records rather than markets.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

A page in a mission baptismal register records a name assigned, a date, and a
parentage. The name the person was born with is not there. One line contains the
whole mechanism, and California's first form of power is visible in it: the
conversion of human lives into administrative entries by an institution that
owned the only pen.

Spain took Alta California from 1769 without a settler population, an economy,
or a market, and held it with a system rather than a settlement. Three
institutions did the work. The presidio supplied force. The pueblo supplied
provisions. And the mission supplied labour and record, which made it the
important one. Mission San Francisco de Asís was founded in 1776 at what is now
320 Dolores Street, in the same season as a declaration on the other coast; the
building is still standing, and it was an accounting office as much as a church.

The strategic object was never conversion for its own sake. It was keeping
Russia and Britain off the Pacific coast, and specifically holding the greatest
natural harbour on it. Everything else was instrumentation around that.

What the registers did was make the population legible. A baptism was an
administrative event with labour consequences: it created an obligation, a
location, and a name that could be tracked. This is a chokepoint on the record
itself, and it is the same position the archive will occupy in Act III and the
platform will occupy in Act V.

The cost is the chapter's centre and not a footnote to it. The Ohlone, Chumash,
and dozens of other peoples appear in California's founding documents almost
exclusively as entries, enumerated and renamed and set to work in an economy
they were not free to leave, and the population collapse in the mission
districts is the defining fact of the period. It is also, awkwardly for the
institution, documented in the institution's own books — the archive contains
the evidence against the archivist, including the records of flight and revolt.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Beats

1. **Hook.** A line in a baptismal register. A name given, a name missing.
2. **The system, not the settlement.** Presidio for force, mission for labour
   and record, pueblo for supply. Three institutions, one machine, and the
   middle one is the important one.
3. **1769 and the northward push.** San Diego, Monterey, then the Bay. Motive:
   keeping Russia and Britain off the Pacific coast, not conversion for its own
   sake.
4. **320 Dolores Street, 1776.** Mission Dolores founded in the same season as a
   declaration on the other coast. Name the address; the book returns to it in
   the epilogue.
5. **The harbour as the real prize.** The Bay is the chokepoint. Everything else
   is instrumentation around it.
6. **Legibility.** What the registers recorded and why. Baptism as an
   administrative event with labour consequences.
7. **Coerced labour.** State it plainly and with the evidence: the mission
   economy ran on Indigenous labour that was not free to leave.
8. **Demographic collapse.** Disease and conditions. Use a sourced range, per
   the research log's rule, and do not round for effect.
9. **Resistance.** Flight, revolt, and the fact that the records document their
   own resistance. The archive contains the evidence against the archivist.
10. **Landing.** California's first power was the power to enumerate. Hand off
   to ch. 2: sovereignty on paper, before there is anything to govern.
:::
